narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your LSAT score, your undergraduate GPA, and your academic performance in the third year of law school. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and worked in your favor: at 39, it sits above the average of students who were accepted, pushing the model toward predicting you would pass the bar. Unfortunately, the other two factors pulled more strongly in the opposite direction. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average among accepted students, and your third-year class ranking placed you in the fourth decile—below the typical fifth-to-sixth decile range of successful applicants. These two academic signals outweighed the positive LSAT result and tipped the overall prediction toward failure.

Your family income, gender, race, and full-time work plans played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT or enrolling in a bar-preparation course that targets first-time passage. Raising your demonstrated academic performance and test scores will directly address the factors that led to this rejection. (218 words)
